How much to charge for crawl space encapsulation

Waterproofing contractors get shopped on a published $4 / sq ft encapsulation Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the liner or the access. A dry 36-inch ranch with 6-mil liner-only is a different job from an 18-inch wet belly crawl with 20-mil wall liner, a commercial dehumidifier, a dedicated circuit, and a debris clean-out.

Open the free crawl space encapsulation bid calculator

Price the liner and the access, not the $4 dump

Encapsulation is a dirt floor, then a scope, then how you reach it. Length times width is the floor. Stem-wall area is the perimeter times height. Liner-only is a dirt cover. A sealed encapsulate adds wall liner and a taped rim. Encapsulate-plus-dehumidifier adds the machine. A hatch is walkable. An 18-inch belly crawl is slower. Standing water is a pump-out.

A liner is not a sealed encapsulate

The cheap special is almost always 6-mil on a dry, walkable ranch, no wall liner, no dehumidifier. A sealed encapsulate is a different crew day. Matching a liner-only per-foot number on a wet encapsulate-and-dehumidifier job is how a sold crawl becomes a two-day loss after the first pump-out.

This is not basement waterproofing

Basement waterproofing is an interior perimeter drain in a finished basement, plus window wells and a sump pit. A French drain is a yard trench. A sump-pump swap is a pit and a discharge. Radon is SSD pipes. Foundation repair is piers as the job. This prices the dirt crawl: liner, access, and extras. Support piers and a dedicated circuit here are line items on an encapsulate, not those other jobs.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the crawl space encapsulation bid calculator. It is not a waterproofing specification, an engineered stamp, a radon or mold clearance, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge for crawl space encapsulation?

Charge from dirt-floor area, scope, access, and extras — not a published $4 / sq ft special. A dry 36-inch ranch with 6-mil liner-only is a different job from an 18-inch wet belly crawl with 20-mil wall liner, a commercial dehumidifier, a dedicated circuit, and a debris clean-out.

Is liner-only the same bid as a sealed encapsulate?

No. Liner-only is a dirt cover. A sealed encapsulate adds wall liner, a taped rim, and usually insulation. Encapsulate-plus-dehumidifier adds the machine and a drain. Matching a liner-only special on a sealed job is how a sold crawl becomes a two-day loss after the first dehumidifier ticket.

How does access change an encapsulation price?

A walkable hatch is a different crew day from an 18-inch belly crawl. Standing water is a pump-out plus mud. The access does not live in a published per-foot dump.

Is this the same as basement waterproofing?

No. Basement waterproofing is an interior perimeter drain in a finished basement, plus window wells and a sump pit. Encapsulation is a dirt crawl: liner, access, and extras. A French drain is a yard trench. A sump-pump swap is a pit and a discharge.

    Common questions

    Why can a competitor advertise “$4 a square foot encapsulation”?

    Usually because the special is written around one specific job, and that job is a preset here: a dry, walkable 36-inch ranch crawl with 6-mil liner-only — no wall liner, no dehumidifier. It really does price low. What the per-square-foot number cannot see is scope, access, water, and extras like a dedicated circuit, support piers, or a debris clean-out. Price your actual crawl beside the special and the gap becomes a list of line items instead of an argument about who is honest.

    Why does a wet, tight crawl cost so much more than a dry, walkable one?

    Because access and water both add hours before the liner even goes down. A 36-inch hatch crawl is the cheap-special assumption. An 18–24 inch belly crawl means the whole job is done lying down. Standing water needs a pump-out before anything else can start. None of that changes how many square feet of liner get cut — it changes how long every one of those feet takes to install.

    What’s the real difference between liner-only, encapsulate, and encapsulate-plus-dehumidifier?

    Liner-only is 6-mil laid loose on the dirt — a vapor barrier and nothing else. Sealed encapsulate adds a wall liner and seals the space, which controls humidity somewhat but does not actively remove it. Adding a commercial dehumidifier is what keeps the space dry through a humid summer rather than just slowing the vapor down. Skipping the dehumidifier on a genuinely wet crawl is how a sealed space ends up growing mold anyway.

    Is this the same as basement waterproofing or foundation repair?

    No. This prices sealing and drying a dirt crawl space — liner, access, insulation, and a dehumidifier. It is distinct from basement waterproofing (an interior perimeter drain and sump pit in a finished basement), a French drain (a yard trench), a sump pump swap, radon mitigation (SSD pipes and a fan), foundation repair (piers holding up a settled structure), mold remediation (containment and clearance testing), spray foam (board-foot insulation as the job), and attic blown-in insulation. A crawl with a genuine structural problem needs a foundation-repair bid, not this one.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your crawl dimensions, wages, or prices.

    What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

    The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — liner, access, insulation, dehumidifier, support piers, and a clean-out — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all. Typing a price you are considering shows you the margin or the loss before you send it.

vs-a-flat-4-dollar-sq-ft-special.html.text:
← Crawl Space Encapsulation Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $4/sq ft encapsulation special

“$4 a square foot” is not a price for a crawl space — it is a price for one specific scope and access, quietly applied to every crawl that calls in.

What a flat $4/sq ft encapsulation special is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote: multiply the crawl's floor area by a number and read off a price. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one crawl — a dry, walkable hatch crawl getting 6-mil liner-only, no wall liner, no dehumidifier — and then reused for every crawl afterward, whether or not the next one looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the floor and stem-wall dimensions, scope (liner-only, sealed encapsulate, or encapsulate plus dehumidifier), access (hatch, tight belly-crawl, or wet), insulation, and extras such as clean-out, support piers, a dedicated circuit, and exterior grading, plus your own labor hours and material costs. It prices the liner, the access premium, and the dehumidifier separately by scope and access type, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this crawl, not a generic one.

What a flat $4/sq ft special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sf whether the scope is 6-mil liner-only or a sealed encapsulation with a wall liner and a rim seal — even though a sealed encapsulation adds wall-liner hours and material that a dirt-only liner never touches. Prices floor liner and wall liner separately by scope, so a sealed encapsulation is never quoted off a liner-only rate.
Has no line for access difficulty, regardless of whether the crawl is a walkable 36-inch hatch or an 18-inch wet belly-crawl needing a pump-out first. Prices access hours and an access premium per square foot by access type — hatch, tight, or wet — so a wet belly-crawl costs more than an easy hatch job of the same footprint.
Has no line for a commercial dehumidifier, its install hours, or the dedicated circuit it needs, regardless of whether the crawl gets one. Prices the dehumidifier invoice, its install hours, and a dedicated-circuit line item separately when scoped, so a fully conditioned crawl costs more than a shell liner.
Has no line for clean-out, support piers, or exterior grading, regardless of how many the crawl needs. Prices clean-out yardage, piers, and grading separately when scoped, so a crawl with real extras is never priced the same as one without.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat rate would have quoted the same crawl, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two crawls, the same footprint-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($32/hr crew wage, 30% burden, $95 travel and equipment, 15% overhead, a 20% target margin):

CrawlThis calculator's priceA flat $4/sq ft special, applied by footprint aloneGap
1,120 sq ft dry ranch, hatch access, 6-mil liner-only — the crawl the flat number is named for$2,453.49 bid price; $1,962.79 break-even cost$4,480.00The flat special runs $2,517.21 over this crawl's own break-even cost, and $2,026.51 over the calculator's own bid price — generous on the cheap end.
864 sq ft wet, tight belly-crawl, sealed encapsulate, 20-mil wall liner, rim foam, 90-pint dehumidifier$11,580.24 bid price; $9,264.20 break-even cost$3,456.00The same $4/sq ft special quotes $5,808.20 below this crawl's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $8,124.24 below the calculator's bid price.

Both flat-rate quotes use the literal $4/sq ft rate named in the calculator's own worked presets, applied to each crawl's own floor area (1,120 sf and 864 sf). The same number that pads the dry hatch crawl's margin by more than half again turns into a five-figure loss the moment access and scope change to wet, sealed, and mechanical — even though a per-square-foot rate has no way to see any of that. Run your own crawl's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one crawl it was built for, and nothing about a per-square-foot number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $4/sq ft encapsulation special get a crawl space quote wrong?

Because the cost driver is scope and access, not floor area alone. Liner-only on a dry, walkable hatch crawl needs a fraction of the labor and material that a sealed encapsulation with a wall liner, a rim seal, and a commercial dehumidifier needs on a wet, 18-inch belly crawl -- none of which scale with square footage the way a flat rate assumes. A $4/sq ft special charges both the same.

What does a flat $4/sq ft encapsulation special usually leave out entirely?

Access difficulty, wall liner, sealing, and a dehumidifier. A dry ranch a crew can stand up in is doing far less than a wet, 18-inch belly crawl that needs a pump-out first, a 20-mil wall liner, rim foam, a dedicated circuit, and a 90-pint dehumidifier running on a drain -- and a per-square-foot number has no line for any of it.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($32/hr crew wage, 30% burden, $95 travel and equipment, 15% overhead, a 20% target margin): a 1,120 sq ft dry ranch with hatch access and 6-mil liner-only costs $1,962.79 to build. The flat $4/sq ft special charges $4,480.00 for that crawl -- $2,517.21 over cost, and $2,026.51 over the calculator's own bid price. Applied to an 864 sq ft wet, tight belly-crawl needing sealed encapsulation, a 20-mil wall liner, rim foam, and a 90-pint dehumidifier, the same $4/sq ft special charges only $3,456.00 -- $5,808.20 below that crawl's own $9,264.20 walk-away cost, before a dollar of profit, and $8,124.24 below the calculator's own bid price.

Is a flat $4/sq ft encapsulation special ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical crawls -- same access, same scope, no dehumidifier either time -- a flat rate can land close, and on this calculator's own cheap-end preset it lands generous. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which crawl it was built on and neither does the estimator until access, scope, and extras are actually spelled out.

Does this calculator know what materials or labor cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates. It takes the crawl's floor and stem-wall dimensions, scope (liner-only, sealed encapsulate, or encapsulate plus dehumidifier), access (hatch, tight belly-crawl, or wet), insulation, and extras, plus your own labor hours and material costs, and turns that into a price for this crawl -- the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

This calculator vs. QuoteIQ

Two different shapes: QuoteIQ is a subscription CRM for running a waterproofing company's leads, estimates, and job costing. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one crawl space cost, given its floor area, liner type, and access, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

QuoteIQ is CRM and estimating software marketed specifically to crawl space encapsulation and waterproofing businesses, alongside basement waterproofing and related trades. Its own marketing describes tiered pricing presets — basic vapor barrier, full encapsulation, and premium conditioned crawl space — satellite-based measurement of a home's footprint and perimeter, job costing, and lead and follow-up tracking. It is sold as an ongoing subscription. QuoteIQ's own current pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — waterproofing-industry CRM and estimating software, sold as a subscription — are stated, and no dollar amount for QuoteIQ appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what QuoteIQ does. It does not track leads, manage a sales pipeline, or measure a home from satellite imagery, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one crawl space's floor area, a choice between liner-only and sealed encapsulation, hatch versus belly-crawl versus wet access, dehumidifier and sump-pump extras, loaded wage, payroll burden, materials, overhead, target margin, and travel, and turns that into the per-job price, the extra-work share, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job.
